Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Baltimore MD/Washington DC
410 PM EST Wed Nov 25 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
Coastal Flood Warnings and Advisories have been issued. The High
Wind Warning was expanded to include western Highland County.
Highlighting the potential for a small area above 3000 feet on
the Allegheny Front to see some freezing rain or even snow
tonight. A Marginal Risk of severe weather was added for far
southern Maryland on Thursday.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
- 1) A powerful coastal low is set to bring hazardous wind,
  tidal flooding, and locally heavy rain on Thanksgiving Day.

- 2) Drier conditions this weekend, followed by additional
  precipitation early next week.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
KEY MESSAGE 1...Seasonably cool today ahead of a powerful
coastal low set to bring hazardous weather on Thanksgiving Day.

A strong dome of Canadian high pressure currently stretches from
the Great Lakes into southern Quebec and New England. Low
pressure approaching southern Florida will lift northward
tonight, eventually bringing significant impacts for
Thanksgiving.

First, as precipitation enters the area tonight, a colder pocket
of air may remain around 3000-4000 feet along the Allegheny
Front. This could result in some freezing rain on some of these
ridgetops. Some guidance even indicates wetbulb cooling could
result in snow as well. Given a limited areal impact, have
covered this threat with a Special Weather Statement in western
Grant and western Pendleton.

There are two key components aloft to consider for this major
pattern change ahead. Multi-channel water vapor imagery depicts
an upper low dropping into the central Plains. A separate 
feature off to the south is currently pushing across the lower 
Mississippi Valley while taking an eastward track toward the 
Gulf Coast. This more southern disturbance is the one that 
begins to gain latitude along the southeastern U.S. coast while 
attaining a negative tilt. This strengthening process will yield
a series of deepening cyclone centers along a wavy occluding 
frontal system. Based on late November climatology, this trough 
exhibits highly anomalous parameters which include its moisture 
content, wind fields, and degree of low-level convergence. This 
high-impact system is expected to impact the local area late 
tonight through Thanksgiving Day.

The intense wind field extends all the way down to the surface
layer. Most guidance even shows 70 to 80 knot wind vectors down
to the 925-mb level. The main question is can any of the gusty
showers bring this intense wind field down to the surface.
Forecast soundings show ample stability in the lower atmosphere
north of the warm/occluded front (with winds quickly decreasing
in its wake), but a few rogue gusts approaching 65 to 75 mph 
are not out of the question, especially along the higher ridges.
For the Alleghenies, downsloping wave breaks are possible along
and west of the crest. Relatively stronger winds are also 
expected along the Chesapeake Bay thanks to reduced friction. 
With the strong winds in place, High Wind Warnings and Wind 
Advisories have been issued for the entire forecast area. These 
generally cover late tonight to the afternoon hours on 
Thanksgiving Day. Most of the region can expect sustained winds 
of 25 to 30 mph with gusts to around 45 to 60 mph. High Wind 
Warnings were not expanded any farther westward due to the 
unfavorable near-surface conditions, but it's worth noting even
small changes in elevation or exposure to the east could 
drastically change what one experiences in terms of wind. The 
driver of the wind will largely be the incredibly tight 
gradients in place, so this will likely be a scenario where 
sustained winds are higher than expected, but gusts fall short 
of raw model-derived output. Any heavier convective elements 
could also play a role in bringing down higher gusts, with this 
threat more plausible near and east of I-95. While leaf fall and
dry ground will be mitigating factors for tree fall, the 
duration of high sustained winds will likely still cause some 
tree damage and power outages.

Besides the wind, a moderate to heavy area of rain lifts 
northward across the area. This first impacts the I-64 corridor 
as soon as midnight, with I-66 around 5-11 AM, and finally I-70
by 6 AM-noon. Rain totals of 1 to 2 inches may fall as this 
activity pushes through. Additional areas of heavy rain are
possible in the afternoon as the low approaches and convective
elements are drawn into the area. High end rain totals could
reach 3 to 4 inches in spots, especially along the Blue Ridge
eastward to southern Maryland. Some sensitive locations could 
see spotty flooding issues if the higher amount is realized, but
felt the risk is isolated enough to preclude a Flood Watch. The
recent dry conditions will certainly act as a limiting factor, 
but leaf-clogged storm drains will serve as a source for poor- 
draining flooding in urban areas. Once the rain shield lifts 
northward during the afternoon and early evening, remaining 
precipitation turns more scattered in nature as the upper trough
passes overhead. 

In summary, anyone traveling from Thanksgiving morning into the
early afternoon should be prepared for adverse or even hazardous
travel due to the heavy rain and strong winds. Be alert for
rapidly changing conditions if you must venture out.

Some surface-based instability may try to work into far southern
Maryland as the triple point low lifts northward. This is the
most favorable area for convective enhanced winds and where SPC
has introduced a Marginal Risk for severe weather. The threat of
a brief tornado/waterspout in any supercell structures likely 
remains south of our forecast area, but is worth monitoring.
While unlikely, a rumble or two of thunder could occur just
about anywhere near and east of the I-95 corridor.

The recent new moon and strong onshore flow will result in minor
to moderate tidal flooding Thursday into Friday as well. See 
section below for more details.

Amidst all the wind and rain, temperatures should be 
on the cooler side due to prevailing northeasterly winds. Expect
highs in the 50s (perhaps briefly spiking into the 60s along
I-95 in the early evening), with mainly 40s west of the Blue 
Ridge. Heading into the night, thick low clouds will hold 
temperatures in the upper 30s to 40s.

The northern upper low eventually crosses the region by early 
Friday. Ample lift underneath this feature will bring some 
scattered showers on Friday morning. This trough will also kick
off upslope rain and snow showers along the Alleghenies. It is 
not the most favorable wind direction which is just south of the
west. The duration and precipitation amounts still remain
uncertain, but the favored west-facing higher elevations could 
end up with a few inches of snow by Saturday morning. For the 
entire area, winds remain elevated with gusts up to 25 to 35 
mph, locally nearing 45 mph in the mountains. The westerly 
component to the winds does help warm temperatures back into the
50s. Cyclonic gradients remain tight into Friday night as lows 
fall into the 30s to low 40s.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Drier conditions this weekend, followed by additional 
precipitation early next week.

High pressure will build across the southern half of our region 
Saturday and Sunday. Temperatures will be near seasonable and 
conditions will be dry. Highs Saturday middle 50s to lower 60s. 
Temperatures will be cooler in the western mountains.

Later in the day Sunday into Sunday night, the high moves to the 
east. At the same time, low pressure over the Middle Mississippi 
Valley will move northeast into the Eastern Great Lakes. The 
interaction between the two will allow for a slight to gradual 
return flow to develop into our region. Highs Sunday will be a few 
degrees warmer reaching the upper 50s to middle 60s. Temperatures 
will be cooler in the western mountains.

A trailing cold front from the low pressure system will move into 
and through our region sometime Sunday night into Monday morning.
Showers could accompany the front mainly Sunday night, but could 
linger Monday morning depending on the forward progression of the 
front. Due to a southerly flow ahead of the front, Sunday night's 
low temperatures could be nearly 10 degrees milder than Saturday 
night's low temperatures. Highs Monday could be the same as Sunday 
reaching the upper 50s to middle 60s, or perhaps a little cooler 
depending on cloud cover, shower coverage and frontal passage timing.

Cool high pressure will build in behind the cold front Monday night 
and Tuesday. Thus, dry conditions return and temperatures will see a 
5 to 10 degree diurnal and nocturnal drop. Highs Tuesday upper 40s 
to middle 50s.

&&

.AVIATION /19Z WEDNESDAY THROUGH MONDAY/...
VFR conditions remain in most areas through this evening with
gradually lowering ceilings, although some MVFR ceilings could
reach CHO by sunset. Increasing northeasterly winds are 
expected to continue overnight. Gusts this evening move into 
the 20 to 30 knot range before reaching 30 to 40 knots near 
sunrise. This comes with the northward push of moderate to 
heavy rains that will impact the terminals in the 06Z-18Z window
(earlier for KCHO and later for KBWI and KMTN). A robust wind 
field brings low-level shear with 55 to 65 kt winds at 2kft AGL.
IFR conditions move in toward daybreak and will likely continue
much of Thanksgiving Day. There will be some breaks in the rain
during the afternoon/evening hours, but there is also a risk of
heavier convective elements during the afternoon to early
evening, especially at the metro terminals. Strong 
northeasterly winds persist into the early afternoon, with a 
steady decrease toward early evening. This may be a case where 
sustained winds are fairly high (potentially in the 30 to 40 kt 
range for a few hours in the morning) with a lower gust factor. 
However, there will still be a risk of 40 to 50 kt gusts at 
times for all terminals. 

After a break as the low passes, winds shift to the southwest 
Thursday evening, and gusts will increase again late Thursday 
night through Friday (up to 30 kt at times). Ceilings likely 
improve to MVFR Thursday night but may not return to VFR until 
Saturday. Some scattered showers may linger through Friday as 
well, especially at MRB. Winds diminish slightly into Friday 
night.

VFR conditions Saturday and Sunday. Brief MVFR conditions could 
unfold Sunday night as rain showers move through some of the 
terminals. Winds west becoming southwest 5 to 10 knots Saturday into 
Saturday night. Winds south 5 to 10 knots Sunday. 

&&

.MARINE...
A prolong period of hazardous marine conditions is expected 
across the region. Stout high pressure across New England is 
leading to a brisk northeasterly winds across the waterways. 
Small Craft Advisories are in effect for all waters today. 
Thereafter, have upgraded to Gale and Storm Warnings for tonight
into Friday. The strong winds will gradually spread from south
to north through the overnight hours. Storm Warnings are in
effect for the entire length of the bay given increasing 
computer model support for 48 to 55 knot gusts. For the middle
and upper tidal Potomac, gales will carry gusts of 40 to 45 
knots, although a few gusts could approach storm force. This 
also includes high waves on the order of 3 to 7 feet. 

There will likely be a lull in the winds Thursday evening as the
low passes, but winds will then turn southwesterly and increase
again overnight into Friday. Gale Warnings continue for the bay
with high end Small Craft Advisories elsewhere. There is still
some uncertainty with the timing and magnitudes of these winds,
but overall should start seeing a decrease by late Friday night.

Small craft advisories likely early Saturday, then fading the 
remainder of the day into Saturday night. No marine hazards Sunday. 
Winds west 10 to 20 knots gusts up to 25 knots Saturday morning, 
diminishing through the rest of the day. Winds becoming southwest 5 
to 15 knots Sunday.

&&

.TIDES/COASTAL FLOODING...
Intense low pressure will move up the coast, with very strong
(near record) high pressure to the north. This results in a
period of strong onshore flow. Tide levels will rapidly rise
tonight into Thursday, with some headline additions possible
depending on how quickly the water rises. The current forecast 
calls for peak anomalies of 3 to 4 feet above normal in the 
middle Chesapeake and Potomac, which combined with high 
astronomical tides from the recent full moon, will result in 
moderate tidal flooding. Coastal Flood Warnings have been issued
for these impacted areas. Coastal Flood Advisories have been 
issued for the rest of the Potomac shoreline where significant 
flooding is less common due to the nature of the shoreline. 
Advisories have also been issued for the remaining northern bay 
shoreline as well. The storm should move quickly enough to 
preclude major flooding anywhere.

The heaviest rain may coincide with high tide around southern
Maryland, furthering the flooding risk due to drainage issues
along the coast with fresh plus tidal input on Thursday.

Winds shift around to the west and southwest Thursday night into
Friday, which isn't the most favorable for water to quickly 
evacuate the bay. Given the high astronomical tides, this could
keep a risk of minor to even moderate tidal flooding in the 
picture through Friday night. The excess anomaly will likely 
build toward the northern reaches of the bay at this time. A 
Coastal Flood Watch has been issued for Havre de Grace due to 
the uncertainty of just how high this surge will be. Tide levels
then drop rapidly Saturday.

&&

alerts.desc:

possible in low lying areas due to tidal flooding.

* WHERE...Shoreline in the District of Columbia, Arlington
County, and the City of Alexandria.

* WHEN...From Thursday afternoon through late Thursday night,
especially around the time of high tide.

* IMPACTS...Water may approach buildings near King Street and
Union Street in Alexandria. Flooding is possible at the DC
seafood market and in portions of East Potomac Park. Water may
cover the boardwalk at Washington Harbour. Low-lying areas near

alerts.headline: Wind Advisory issued November 25 at 1:48AM EST until November 26 at 4:00PM EST by NWS Baltimore MD/Washington DC
alerts.desc:
* WHAT...Northeast winds 20 to 30 mph with gusts up to 55 mph
expected.

* WHERE...District of Columbia, central, north central, northeast,
northern, southern, and western Maryland, northern and northwest
Virginia, and eastern and panhandle West Virginia.

* WHEN...From 4 AM to 4 PM EST Thursday.

* IMPACTS...Gusty winds will blow around unsecured objects. Tree
limbs could be blown down and a few power outages may result.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...The combination of a soaking rain and very
windy conditions could result in many downed trees.

* WHERE...Shoreline in the District of Columbia, Arlington
